newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon banks freed from compulsory t-bill buying.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon banks freed from compulsory t-bill buying.

text.p: Lebanon's central bank on Wednesday exempted banks from compulsory subscription of 40 percent of their Lebanese pound deposits in t-bills, to help funnel the funds to the private sector and boost the economy.

The Bank of Lebanon said in a statement that the step, announced after the weekly meeting of the Bank's Central Council grouping Governor Riad Salameh and his four deputies, would free substantial bank funds for public and private sector use.
High investments in pound-denominated treasury bills in recent years have been blamed for soaking up liquidity and were partly responsible for an economic slowdown in 1996.

"Governor Riad Salameh announced after the meeting that the Council has decided to exempt commercial banks from compulsory subscription of 40 percent of their pound deposits in treasury bills. The decision means that any bank is no longer bound to invest in regular bills," the Bank of Lebanon said.
According to the Lebanese Banks Association grouping 79 of Lebanon's 81 commercial banks, the banks total Lebanese pound deposits stood at 13,636 billion pounds at the end of 1996.

The decision came a day after the Banks Association cut the pound prime rate to 16 percent from 18 percent, bringing it almost in line with one- and two-year bill yields. This makes customer loans as interesting to banks as t-bill investment.
The Bank said its Central Council reached the decision following the relief it felt over the monetary situation in Lebanon and the treasury accounts' solvency.
Salameh said the decision would have a positive impact on the economy "because it frees important funds that the public or private sector can benefit from," the Bank added.

"The decision also carries encouraging results pertaining to the banking sector as it forms a step towards the liberation of deposits in the Lebanese currency from any administrative or governmental chains," the statement added.
Freddy Baz, a director of Banque Audi, said the Bank's action was in line with its recent policy of lowering t-bill yields and would lead to a faster decrease in pound rates.
"The step is a sign from the central bank to the banks that says 'I do not need your pounds and see how you can invest them in the market'," Baz told Reuters.

"This action is 100 percent in line with the central bank's adopted policy of lowering interest rates and whose ultimate aim is to liberate banks resources to the private sector and to boost economic growth," Baz added.

But another banker said although the removal of the mandatory t-bill subscriptions was a sign of market stability it would not boost private sector borrowing in the local currency as the pound rates were too high.

"This step itself will not have a major effect as many banks had 80 or 90 percent of their deposits in t-bills anyway," Bassam Yammine, Senior Officer Corporate Finance at Beirut investment house Lebanon Invest, added.

"However previous measures by the central bank, like cutting t-bill yields and the limitations on subscriptions in three- and six-month bills will help pound rates to go down and encourage the private sector to borrow in pounds," Yammine said.
($1 = 1,552 Lebanese pounds at the end of 1996)
